title: Integrals Giving Exponentials and Logarithms
short: ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C and ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C.
trouble: Students drop the absolute value in ln|x|, or apply ∫ 1/x dx to 1/x².

blocks.html: The reverse power rule fails for exactly one power: $x^{-1}$ would need division by 0. The derivative $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}$ from Derivatives of Exponential and Log Functions fills the gap, and Integration by Substitution extends it to a whole family of integrals.

$$\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln\lvert x \rvert + C, \qquad \int e^x\,dx = e^x + C, \qquad \int a^x\,dx = \frac{a^x}{\ln a} + C,$$ and by substitution $\displaystyle\int\frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}\,dx = \ln\lvert g(x) \rvert + C$ (top = derivative of the bottom).

For $x > 0$, $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}$. For $x < 0$, $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(-x) = \frac{-1}{-x} = \frac{1}{x}$ as well. The absolute value combines both cases, so $\ln\lvert x \rvert$ is an antiderivative of $\frac{1}{x}$ on each side of 0. Without the absolute value, the formula would be undefined for every negative $x$, where $\frac{1}{x}$ is perfectly happy.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $\int_{-3}^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ is the shaded region below the axis: its value is $\ln 1 - \ln 3 = -\ln 3$, using $\ln\lvert x \rvert$.

blocks.title: Top is the derivative of the bottom
steps: $u = x^2 + 4$, $x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}du$: $\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2 + 4) + C$ (no absolute value needed, since $x^2 + 4 > 0$).
$\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$; with $u = \cos x$, $du = -\sin x\,dx$: $-\int\frac{du}{u} = -\ln\lvert\cos x\rvert + C$.

head: Integrand
Antiderivative
blocks.cap: Antiderivatives built from exponentials and logarithms. Each comes from a substitution.

blocks.html: Two slips: dropping the absolute value in $\ln\lvert x \rvert$, and using the log rule where it does not belong. $\int\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ is not $\ln(x^2)$; it is $-\frac{1}{x} + C$ by the power rule. Check by differentiating: $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(x^2) = \frac{2}{x}$, which is not $\frac{1}{x^2}$.
